lesson.title: Reisen II: die Fahrkarte, der Fahrplan, die Abfahrt, die Ankunft, der Flughafen
lesson.subtitle: the timetable set — German compounds it from three verbs, English borrowed it from Latin

hook.title: A Timetable Made of Verbs
hook.content: Look at what English did: departure is Latin dis- + partire, 'to divide apart' — you 'divide' yourself from the journey — and arrival from Vulgar Latin adripare, 'to reach the shore', so English speakers arrive by boat whether or not there is water. German built the same two ideas from strong verbs you already own. fahren gives die Fahrkarte and der Fahrplan as plain compounds, and with the prefix ab- — the same ancient word as English off and Latin ab — it gives die Abfahrt, the off-drive. kommen gives die Ankunft: an + Kunft, and Kunft is kommen frozen into a noun, a living German word until the early 1800s, now surviving only inside compounds like Ankunft and Zukunft. And fliegen's noun compounds with der Hafen — English haven's twin — into der Flughafen. No Latin was borrowed: German made its timetable the Germanic way, by freezing verbs.

footnotes.title: die Fahrt Is fare
footnotes.content: die Fahrt is fahren's journey-noun, and English fare — sea fare, taxi fare, the price of going — is the same noun from the same verb: Old English faru, from faran. Every time you pay a fare you are speaking die Fahrt.

pattern.title: The Timetable in Frames
pattern.content: Four frames. 1. Ticket: Ich kaufe eine Fahrkarte (I buy a ticket) — a fahren-compound, not a new word. 2. Plan: Der Fahrplan ist an der Wand (the timetable is on the wall). 3. Clock: Die Abfahrt ist um acht Uhr, die Ankunft ist spät — um is the clock preposition, and the Abfahrt/Ankunft pair answers leave and arrive without a verb in sight. 4. Fly: Der Flughafen ist sehr groß — fliegen's noun + the harbor word you own; and when the plane joins the timetable, Das Flugzeug ist spät.
pattern.linguist_note: The -t noun is a shared Germanic trick: take a strong verb's participle stem and bolt on t. English built flight from fly (flug- + t) and thought from think; German built Kunft from kommen and Zucht from ziehen. German then let standalone Kunft die in the 1800s — it survives inside Ankunft, Zukunft, Auskunft, Herkunft. English kept flight and never had Kunft: same construction, opposite fates.

exercises.prompt: The timetable set — match each sentence with its reading:

matching_pairs.english: The timetable is on the wall
matching_pairs.german: Der Fahrplan ist an der Wand

matching_pairs.english: The departure is at eight o'clock
matching_pairs.german: Die Abfahrt ist um acht Uhr

matching_pairs.english: The hotel is near the airport
matching_pairs.german: Das Hotel ist in der Nähe vom Flughafen

matching_pairs.english: The bus drives to the stop
The departure is in June, the arrival is in November
matching_pairs.german: Die Abfahrt ist im Juni, die Ankunft ist im November

matching_pairs.english: The date is on the ticket
matching_pairs.german: Das Datum steht auf der Fahrkarte

matching_pairs.english: Rolls with jam for the trip
matching_pairs.german: Brötchen mit Marmelade für die Fahrt

exercises.target_answer: Ich kaufe eine Fahrkarte, Der Fahrplan ist an der Wand, Die Abfahrt ist um acht Uhr, Die Ankunft ist spät, Der Flughafen ist sehr groß, Das Flugzeug ist spät, Das Hotel ist in der Nähe vom Flughafen, Mein Koffer ist schwer, Der Bus fährt zur Haltestelle, Die Abfahrt ist im Juni, die Ankunft ist im November, Das Datum steht auf der Fahrkarte, Brötchen mit Marmelade für die Fahrt
exercises.meaning: ticket, timetable, departure, arrival, airport, plane
exercises.explanation: Most of these sentences hang on compounds or frozen verbs: Fahrkarte, Fahrplan, Abfahrt, Ankunft, Flughafen. Only kaufe and ist do plain work — the timetable is a family tree of fahren, kommen and fliegen.

exercises.prompt: 'Die Ankunft' is the arrival — an + Kunft. Which strong verb is frozen inside it?
exercises.meaning: Ankunft = an + Kunft, the old noun of kommen
exercises.explanation: Kunft is kommen frozen into a noun — independent German until the early 1800s, now alive only inside Ankunft and Zukunft. English did the same freezing on fliegen's twin: see the next exercise.

exercises.prompt: Ankunft ends in Kunft — kommen frozen into a noun with the -t ending. English built one word exactly the same way from fly. Which?
exercises.meaning: Kunft ↔ flight: the same -t noun on a strong verb
exercises.explanation: fly's participle stem flug- plus t gives flight — precisely how kommen gives Kunft. The -ight words are look-alikes: fright, light and fight come from different verbs entirely. English kept flight and never had Kunft; German kept Kunft, but only inside compounds.

exercises.prompt: Assemble the timetable pair: 'The departure is early, the arrival is late'
exercises.target_answer: Die Abfahrt ist früh, die Ankunft ist spät
exercises.meaning: The departure is early, the arrival is late
exercises.explanation: The leave/arrive pair, no verb in sight: Abfahrt (ab + Fahrt) takes früh, Ankunft (an + Kunft) takes spät. Both nouns are feminine, and both carry a strong verb frozen inside them.

exercises.prompt: Assemble: 'The ticket for the train is expensive'
exercises.target_answer: Die Fahrkarte für den Zug ist teuer
exercises.meaning: The ticket for the train is expensive
exercises.explanation: für takes the accusative: für den Zug. teuer is the d→t twin of English dear — the Tag/day family again — and the bank's Fahrplan and schnell are there to prove Fahrkarte stays a compound even in a longer frame.

summary.outcome: Read a German timetable: know which verb each of Fahrkarte, Fahrplan, Abfahrt, Ankunft and Flughafen freezes.

use_example.german: Die Abfahrt ist um acht Uhr — die Ankunft ist spät.
use_example.english: The departure is at eight o'clock — the arrival is late.

summary.takeaway: Abfahrt = ab (English off) + Fahrt (fare); Ankunft = an + Kunft, kommen's frozen noun and flight's twin; Flughafen = Flug + Hafen (haven). English borrowed Latin for all of it.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: the day-trip kit — der Ausflug, der Tourist, das Gepäck, der Pass, die Fähre.

twist.prompt: Without looking back — rebuild the core sentence from Reisen II: die Fahrkarte, der Fahrplan, die Abfahrt, die Ankunft, der Flughafen (The ticket for the train is expensive):
twist.target_answer: Die Fahrkarte für den Zug ist teuer
twist.explanation: Re-assembling "Die Fahrkarte für den Zug ist teuer" from scratch locks in the structural pattern of Reisen II: die Fahrkarte, der Fahrplan, die Abfahrt, die Ankunft, der Flughafen without relying on short-term echo.

fahrkarte.context_phrase: Ich kaufe eine Fahrkarte nach Berlin.
fahrkarte.context_translation: I buy a ticket to Berlin.
fahrkarte.etymology_derivation: fahren (to travel, the fare root) + Karte (card, from Latin charta — the same loan as English card): a travel-card. [wiktionary]

fahrplan.context_phrase: Der Fahrplan hängt an der Wand.
fahrplan.context_translation: The timetable hangs on the wall.
fahrplan.etymology_derivation: fahren (to drive, the fare root) + Plan (plan, the same French-Latin word English uses): the travel-plan, a timetable. [wiktionary]

abfahrt.context_phrase: Die Abfahrt ist um neun Uhr.
abfahrt.context_translation: The departure is at nine o'clock.
abfahrt.etymology_derivation: The noun of abfahren: ab (off) + Fahrt (the fare root) — literally an off-driving, a departure. [wiktionary]

ankunft.context_phrase: Die Ankunft ist um halb sieben.
ankunft.context_translation: The arrival is at half past six.
ankunft.etymology_derivation: From ankommen (to arrive) — an on-coming; kommen is the German twin of come. [wiktionary]

flughafen.etymology_derivation: Flug (flight) + Hafen (port) — the flight-port; see der Fernseher-style calques. [wiktionary]

nähe.context_phrase: In der Nähe gibt es einen Markt.
nähe.etymology_derivation: nah + -e; nah is the twin of archaic English nigh. [wiktionary]

koffer.etymology_derivation: Through Middle Dutch from Old French cofre — the French loan English also took as coffer and coffin. [wiktionary]

haltestelle.context_translation: The bus stop is right here.
haltestelle.etymology_derivation: halten (to hold) + Stelle (place, from the same old place-root as English stall): a hold-place, where the vehicle stops. [wiktionary]

hotel.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from French hôtel — the same French loan as English hotel. [wiktionary]

taxi.context_phrase: Wir nehmen ein Taxi zum Hotel.
taxi.context_translation: We take a taxi to the hotel.
taxi.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from French taxi, the cab named for its taximeter — the identical French word English uses. [wiktionary]

bus.context_phrase: Der Bus kommt um acht Uhr.
bus.context_translation: The bus comes at eight o'clock.
bus.etymology_derivation: From Omnibus, the Latin for-all vehicle, shortened with influence from English bus — both languages took the same Latin dative. [wiktionary]

theater.context_translation: We are going to the theater today.
theater.etymology_derivation: From French théâtre, from Latin theātrum, from Greek theātron (a place for viewing) — the same viewing-place word English took as theater. [wiktionary]

kino.context_translation: We are going to the cinema.
kino.etymology_derivation: Clipping of Kinematograph, the Greek-rooted invention name — a shared international loan. [wiktionary]

juni.etymology_derivation: Latin loan both English and German borrowed (via French): Latin Iūnius. [wiktionary]

november.etymology_derivation: Latin loan both languages share: Latin November, inherited via Middle High German. [wiktionary]

dauern.etymology_derivation: From Latin dūrō via Middle Low German — kin to archaic English dure, as in endure. [wiktionary]

datum.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from Latin datum, literally something given — the same Latin participle that gave English date, from the Roman letter formula given at Rome. [wiktionary] [etymonline]

brötchen.context_phrase: Ich kaufe jeden Morgen frische Brötchen.
brötchen.context_translation: I buy fresh rolls every morning.
brötchen.etymology_derivation: Brötchen — diminutive of Brot (bread), which is cognate with English bread; both trace to PIE *bʰrewh₁-, the root of brew. [wiktionary]

marmelade.etymology_derivation: Marmelade — 16th century, from Middle French marmelade, from Portuguese marmelada (quince jam); English marmalade took the same route. [wiktionary]

toast.etymology_derivation: Toast — borrowed straight from English toast, with toasten and Toaster as later German offshoots. [wiktionary]

butterbrot.context_phrase: Ich nehme ein Butterbrot mit in die Schule.
butterbrot.context_translation: I take a sandwich to school.
butterbrot.etymology_derivation: Butter + Brot — both elements are documented twins (Butter via Latin butyrum, Brot kin to brew); an exact internal calque. [wiktionary]

frühstück.context_phrase: Das Frühstück ist um sieben Uhr.
frühstück.etymology_derivation: Literally 'early piece (bite)': früh + Stück; NOT the break-fast calque English uses. [wiktionary]

zimmer.context_phrase: Mein Zimmer ist groß und hell.
zimmer.context_translation: My room is big and bright.
zimmer.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *timrą — cognate with English timber: English keeps t, German shifted it to z. [wiktionary]

tasche.etymology_derivation: Perhaps Proto-Germanic *taskǭ; no English cognate — memorize this one. [wiktionary]

fahren.context_translation: I am going / driving to Berlin.
fahren.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *faraną — the twin of English fare (farewell, bus fare, 'how did you fare?'). [wiktionary]

fahrt.etymology_derivation: Noun of fahren (fare): a 'faring' — a drive, ride, or voyage; the -t is the Germanic -þ nominal suffix. [wiktionary]

fliegen.context_translation: We are flying to Rome tomorrow.
fliegen.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *fleuganą (PIE *plewk-) — English fly is the documented cognate; strong verb: flog, geflogen. [wiktionary]

hafen.context_translation: The ship is lying in the harbor.
hafen.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *habno — the page lists English haven as the direct cognate: a harbor is a haven. [wiktionary]

zug.etymology_derivation: Noun of ziehen (to pull — the tow/tug family): a train is 'the pull(er)', an elevator the Aufzug ('up-pull'). [wiktionary]

uhr.etymology_derivation: Loan-cognate of hour (Latin hōra via French), and a distant doublet of Jahr and year (PIE *yóh₁r̥). German alone turned it into the word for the clock itself. [wiktionary]

flugzeug.etymology_derivation: Flug (flight, from fliegen — English fly) + Zeug (gear, as in Feuerzeug): the fly-gear. [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
